title: Public Investment in CPAT
subtitle: Investment needs, the cost of capital and the efficiency of public spending
message: The cost of capital, not the size of the bill, decides whether developing-country climate investment pays its way. A stylized clean asset fails above 12.6 percent, almost exactly CPAT's default for lower-middle-income countries; a spending test shows the budget's problem is often liquidity, not value.

problem.text: CPAT's power model reports investment at default costs of capital of 7.5 to 15 percent, but outside power it has no capital, no payer split and no test of whether public money should pay.

mechanism.title: Three lenses on the same investment
mechanism.caption: Net benefit of one year's 2030 investment, US$ bn a year (stylized savings).
points: Developing countries barely gain at market rates; at 6% they gain $131bn.
Spend public money where its value per dollar beats the cost of raising it (about 1.2).
A PPA priced above the government's rate is debt in disguise.

action.title: Price capital, then test the budget
results: Island case: a $108m plant fails on a 7-year loan; concessional finance or a guaranteed PPA rescues it.
Kenya and Uganda: the increment pays only when cleaner air counts.
Country results are illustrative tool output.
